notes.bp: A spoken-language model needs compact speech units that preserve phonetic content while ignoring who spoke and small recording changes.
notes.wh: Raw waveforms contain speaker, channel, and linguistic variation at the same time; a token that keeps all of it is hard for a language model to reuse.
notes.naive: Cluster acoustic frames directly and assume the most frequent clusters are good linguistic units.
notes.ap: Use double-codebook speaker-invariant clustering to retain phonetic structure while suppressing speaker variation, then test whether the resulting tokens are easy to model and resynthesize.
notes.mech: SpinHuBERT supplies the speech representation and DC-Spin separates speaker-invariant and phonetic information into codebooks; the tokens are tested in zero-shot spoken-language tasks and resynthesis.
notes.math: Clustering assigns nearby representation vectors to discrete symbols; speaker-invariance changes the training objective so distance caused by identity matters less than distance caused by phonetic content.
notes.ww: The paper reports that tokens with phoneme alignment or simple language-model structure are useful downstream and improve the tested zero-shot and resynthesis proxies.
notes.limits: The tokenizers, languages, proxy tasks, and resynthesis setup bound the result; token usefulness is not the same as complete spoken meaning.
notes.title: DC-Spin: A Speaker-invariant Speech Tokenizer for Spoken Language Models

notes.bp: An ASR system should recognize a rare name or domain word when the user supplies a large list of likely terms.
notes.wh: A list of 200,000 candidates can help one word but also create homophone confusion and unacceptable search cost.
notes.naive: Insert the entire bias list into decoding or fine-tune the recognizer for each new list.
notes.ap: Retrieve a small relevant candidate set from speech and bias text, train against homophone confusion, and inject only the retrieved candidates without retraining the recognizer.
notes.mech: Speech-and-bias contrastive learning ranks relevant entries; a dynamic curriculum trains the system on increasingly difficult homophones; pruning then supplies a compact list to the ASR decoder.
notes.math: Contrastive learning pulls matching speech/list pairs together and pushes distractors apart; retrieval converts a huge candidate set into a small conditional search problem.
notes.ww: The paper reports 2.8%/7.1% biased WER with 2,000 words, only 0.3/2.9% absolute degradation at 200,000 entries, 99.99% pruning, and 20 ms query latency on the tested split.
notes.limits: The reported latency, languages, bias lists, and ASR systems define the boundary; rare names outside the retrieval distribution and interactive user correction remain open.
notes.title: BR-ASR: Efficient and Scalable Bias Retrieval Framework for Contextual Biasing ASR in Speech LLM

notes.bp: Meeting transcription must determine both what was said and which person said it when cameras, microphones, overlap, and devices disagree.
notes.wh: Recognition and speaker assignment fail together under overlap, and a separate audio-only pipeline cannot use visible mouth and body evidence.
notes.naive: Transcribe the mixed audio first and attach speaker labels afterward.
notes.ap: Fuse audio and video across diarization, recognition, and joint diarization-recognition tasks, then compare systems under a shared challenge protocol.
notes.mech: MISP 2025 defines AVSD, AVSR, and AVDR tasks with multi-device meeting data; systems combine acoustic and visual streams and are scored on speaker attribution and transcription.
notes.math: Diarization error counts missed, false, and incorrectly attributed speech; character error measures transcript edits; concatenated minimum-permutation error resolves arbitrary speaker-label names.
notes.ww: The challenge reports DER 8.09%, CER 9.48%, and cpCER 11.56% for its top systems, with the largest gain in the joint task.
notes.limits: Challenge data, camera placement, meeting types, language, and leaderboard protocols define the claim; deployment in unseen rooms or privacy-constrained camera settings remains open.
notes.title: The Multimodal Information Based Speech Processing (MISP) 2025 Challenge: Audio-Visual Diarization and Recognition

notes.bp: A screening system should use speech to flag possible adolescent suicide risk when interviews and expert time are limited.
notes.wh: Risk is continuous and multidimensional, while speech carries both acoustic behavior and what the person says; one feature family can miss the other.
notes.naive: Train one binary classifier on a single acoustic summary and treat its score as a clinical decision.
notes.ap: Combine acoustic and semantic features across several task models, then use a nested voting ensemble to stabilize the prediction.
notes.mech: OpenSmile and Emotion2Vec supply acoustic representations, a fine-tuned Chinese BERT supplies semantic features, and XGBoost/SVM-style base models are combined after Bayesian hyperparameter search.
notes.math: An ensemble votes across partially different predictors; recall and F1 expose the cost of missing risk more directly than accuracy alone.
notes.ww: On 600 Chinese adolescents, the paper reports test accuracy .63, recall .74, and F1 about .67.
notes.limits: This is a screening model on one challenge dataset, not a diagnosis or safety-tested intervention; age, language, labels, privacy, calibration, and external validation constrain the claim.
notes.title: Predicting Adolescent Suicidal Risk from Multi-task-based Speech: An Ensemble Learning Approach

notes.bp: A videoconference system should detect moments when a group conversation becomes awkward or stops feeling enjoyable.
notes.wh: The moments are rare and expensive to label, and the signal is distributed across voice, face, and words.
notes.naive: Train a fully supervised multimodal model and label every clip.
notes.ap: Use a small labeled set to teach a model from a larger targeted unlabeled set through semi-supervised co-training.
notes.mech: Audio, facial-action, and text features are fused; modality-specific learners exchange pseudo-label information while the model is tested on held-out sessions.
notes.math: Co-training uses agreement between views to expand supervision; ROC-AUC measures ranking of rare events while F1 measures the chosen decision threshold.
notes.ww: The paper reports ROC-AUC .90 and F1 .60, and says 8% labeled data reaches 96% of the full supervised model's performance.
notes.limits: The labels, videoconference setting, participant population, and definition of negative experience bound the result; detection is not a causal explanation of why a conversation deteriorated.
notes.title: Multimodal Fusion with Semi-Supervised Learning Minimizes Annotation Quantity for Modeling Videoconference Conversation Experience

notes.bp: A cochlear-implant listener may understand speech in competing talkers differently when the target and masker use different languages.
notes.wh: The useful target and competing voices overlap, and the listener's hearing device changes which acoustic cues survive.
notes.naive: Measure speech in quiet or use one same-language masker and assume the result transfers.
notes.ap: Compare electric-acoustic stimulation with implant-only simulation under Mandarin, Cantonese, and English two-talker maskers.
notes.mech: Mandarin sentences are mixed with language-controlled babble, processed by noise vocoders simulating CI or EAS hearing, and scored through sentence recognition.
notes.math: Release from masking is the difference in recognition between a target with and without a linguistic advantage; comparing those differences separates hearing mode from masker language.
notes.ww: The study reports a combined-stimulation advantage across all three masker languages and language-specific differences in release from masking.
notes.limits: Normal-hearing listeners, vocoder simulations, Mandarin targets, and the selected masker languages limit direct claims about real CI users and everyday rooms.
notes.title: Linguistic Masking and Its Release in Simulated Electric-acoustic Hearing

notes.bp: An audio-visual model should connect what an event sounds like, what it looks like, and what language describes it without requiring every video to be manually labeled.
notes.wh: Unlabeled videos contain weak and sometimes misleading cross-modal matches, so training on arbitrary audio-caption pairs can teach the wrong correspondence.
notes.naive: Use one modality pair or trust automatically generated captions without filtering them.
notes.ap: Generate frame captions, filter audio-caption pairs with a CLAP similarity check, and train a text-guided contrastive masked autoencoder over audio, video, and text.
notes.mech: A pretrained text encoder guides masked audio-visual reconstruction and contrastive learning; automatically formed triplets are used for retrieval and classification tests.
notes.math: Contrastive loss pulls matching modalities together and separates mismatches; masking forces the remaining views to predict missing information rather than copy it.
notes.ww: The paper reports up to 5.6% recall@10 improvement for retrieval and 3.2% for classification.
notes.limits: The video domains, caption generator, CLAP filter, and downstream tasks define the result; spoken conversation and human annotation quality outside those videos remain open.
notes.title: Language-Guided Contrastive Audio-Visual Masked Autoencoder with Automatically Generated Audio-Visual-Text Triplets from Videos

notes.bp: ASR should transcribe disordered and dysarthric speech rather than silently serving only speakers whose voices match ordinary training data.
notes.wh: Impaired speech is variable and scarce, and disfluencies can be mistaken for recognition errors or erased by a system tuned for fluent speech.
notes.naive: Apply a high-performing typical-speech recognizer and compare only its overall WER.
notes.ap: Evaluate strong contextual ASR architectures on a dedicated impaired-speech corpus and inspect whether their different context mechanisms help.
notes.mech: ContextNet and Parakeet are tested on Speech Accessibility Project challenge subsets; WER is compared across the challenge conditions.
notes.math: Word error rate counts substitutions, insertions, and deletions; it turns a listener's transcription burden into a measurable but incomplete quantity.
notes.ww: The paper reports WER 10.06% and 11.8% on the two test subsets, with Parakeet slightly ahead of ContextNet.
notes.limits: Challenge data, speaker impairment profiles, transcripts, and WER define the boundary; fairness across disorders, user control, and clinical usefulness remain unestablished.
notes.title: Towards Inclusive and Fair ASR: Insights from the SAPC Challenge for Optimizing Disordered Speech Recognition
